pricing model: Argues from what paid plans cost or how licensing is structured - per-seat rates, tier jumps, add-on billing, price rises, total cost of ownership.
free tier: Argues from the no-cost plan specifically - what it includes or caps, and which limits force teams onto a paid plan.
scalability: Argues from whether performance holds up as issues, projects, users or automations grow - lag, board load times, tuning for large volumes.
integrations ecosystem: Argues from prebuilt connectors, marketplace apps and plugins (GitHub, Slack, CI) - breadth of ready-made links, not the programmatic interface itself.
automation capabilities: Argues from rule engines that act automatically - triggers, conditions, branching, run quotas - not from manually configurable fields or workflows.
reporting depth: Argues from analytics output - dashboards, velocity and portfolio rollups, cross-project reports - not from capturing the underlying time or data.
agile support: Argues from scrum and scaled-agile mechanics - sprints, backlogs, story points, releases, SAFe - excluding pure flow boards and date-based timelines.
gantt support: Argues from date-based timeline or roadmap views with bars, milestones and schedule slippage, as distinct from sprint planning or column boards.
kanban boards: Argues from flow-board mechanics - columns, swimlanes, card configuration, WIP limits, continuous pull - rather than sprint cadence or timelines.
task hierarchy: Argues from vertical nesting of work items (initiative to epic to story to subtask), per-level rules and rollups up the tree.
dependency management: Argues from lateral links between items or teams - blockers, cross-squad dependency maps, risk visibility - not parent-child nesting.
time tracking: Argues from capturing or measuring time on work - worklogs, estimates versus actuals, cycle-time measurement - not from the reports that display it.
resource management: Argues from planning people rather than tasks - capacity, workload balancing, allocation across teams, staffing and financial resource planning.
permissions granularity: Argues from how finely access to work can be scoped - roles, project and issue-level permission schemes, guest and private-project control.
security compliance: Argues from security and governance assurances - SSO/SAML/SCIM, audit logs, encryption, certifications like SOC 2 or HIPAA - not everyday access scoping.
uptime reliability: Argues from service availability - SLAs, outages, vendor track record for staying up - as distinct from speed under heavy load.
customer support: Argues from the vendor's help offering - support tiers, responsiveness, documentation, training, community and practitioner forums.
onboarding speed: Argues from how fast teams get productive - learning curve, sane defaults, templates, setup and admin effort before value appears.
customization level: Argues from manual configurability - custom fields, statuses, workflows per type, schemes, templates - and whether that flexibility helps or bloats.
mobile experience: Argues from use on phones or tablets - the mobile app's quality, coverage or controls - which rarely decides anything here.
api access: Argues from programmatic access - REST/GraphQL APIs, webhooks, rate limits, developer platforms for building custom integrations rather than installing existing ones.
deployment flexibility: Argues from hosting choice - Cloud versus Data Center or self-hosted, data residency, regional or government cloud options.
